traits: Irregularly shaped, slowly enlarging patches of yellowing, thinning or wilted turf
Roots are short, stubby and cropped off an inch or less below the surface
Turf under the patch feels thin and pulls up with little resistance
Damage worsens in the same sandy areas year after year

copy.what_it_means: A slowly enlarging patch of thin, yellowing turf with short, stubby roots can suggest sting nematode, but a photo cannot tell it apart from drought, compaction or a root disease. The only confirmation is a soil sample sent to a lab; a technician collects it.
copy.fact: Sting nematode feeds on root tips from outside the root and is considered the most damaging nematode on Florida lawns.

tech_notes: Ectoparasitic; feeds on root tips from outside the root. Collect 12-16 cores to 4 inches depth from the margin of declining turf (not the dead center) for a nematode assay; rule out drought, compaction and take-all root rot first.

review.notes: Peak months are a general warm-season estimate; UF/IFAS residential lawn nematode guidance gives no Florida-specific seasonal calendar for sting nematode, so season_basis is set to unverified.

symptoms: Irregularly shaped, slowly enlarging patches of yellowing, wilted or thinning turf
Roots are short, stubby and cropped off an inch or less below the surface

required_signature.text: No photo confirms sting nematode. The only confirmation is a soil sample submitted to a nematode assay lab.
elements: Irregularly shaped, slowly enlarging patches of yellowing, wilted or thinning turf

differentials.difference: Take-all root rot roots are short and turn black with a rotted look; sting nematode roots are short and stubby but do not blacken or rot.
differentials.next_observation: A technician compares a pulled root sample under magnification, or a lab distinguishes the two directly.

differentials.difference: White grub turf lifts like a loose mat over grubs feeding on roots; sting nematode turf is thin with shortened roots but no grubs underneath.
differentials.next_observation: A plug pull at the margin, or a technician checks beneath the turf for grubs.

differentials.difference: Chinch bug damage stays in hot, sunny spots with insects present; sting nematode damage spreads more slowly with no insects found.
differentials.next_observation: Pour soapy water on the edge of the patch and watch for small black-and-white bugs climbing up in a few minutes, or a technician checks.

condition.recovery_note: Recovery depends on the assay result and is often slow, over months, as damaged roots regrow.

traits: Thin, slow-to-recover turf in patches, often yellowing or unthrifty
Roots are short with few feeder roots and dead-looking tips
Damage builds slowly and is worse under heat or drought stress
Mostly reported on St. Augustinegrass and bermudagrass

copy.what_it_means: Thin, slow-to-recover turf with short roots can suggest lance nematode, but a photo cannot tell it apart from drought, compaction or a root disease. The only confirmation is a lab soil sample; a technician collects it following the lab protocol.
copy.fact: Lance nematodes are described by UF/IFAS as the major nematode pest of St. Augustinegrass in the southeast.

tech_notes: Sample per the receiving lab's turf protocol before any product; rule out drought, compaction and root disease first. Do not diagnose from a photo.

review.notes: Draft for owner catalog review (2026-09-30 yard-rotation species set). season_basis unverified: IN390 gives no Florida monthly calendar, so peak_months are empty. IN390 does not describe sampling steps; it points to the UF/IFAS nematode management guides.

symptoms: Patches of thin, yellowing or unthrifty turf that recover slowly

elements: Patches of thin, yellowing or unthrifty turf that recover slowly

differentials.difference: Lance nematode roots look short with dead tips; root-knot nematode can leave small galls on roots, though only a lab tells the two apart.
differentials.next_observation: A technician submits a sample per the lab protocol, since only the assay separates them.

traits: Yellowing, wilting or thinning turf despite irrigation
Small galls on the roots on some grasses, with rotting roots below them
Weeds often move into thinning patches
Reported on bermudagrass, zoysia, St. Augustinegrass, bahia and other turf

copy.what_it_means: Yellowing and wilting turf that does not respond to irrigation can suggest root-knot nematode, but a photo cannot tell it apart from drought, compaction or root disease. The only confirmation is a lab test, and a technician follows the lab's turf sampling method.
copy.fact: A routine soil sample can miss grass root-knot nematode because it sits in the thatch and upper inch of soil, which is why the lab asks for turf plugs.

tech_notes: Follow the lab's turf root-knot protocol: turf plugs including thatch and the top inch of soil for mist extraction; a routine soil sample can miss it. Rule out drought, compaction and root disease first.

review.notes: Draft for owner catalog review (2026-09-30 yard-rotation species set). season_basis unverified: IN1231 gives no monthly calendar. symptoms: General decline, stunting and yellowing in irregular patches
